13.reason: Both love (A) and revenge (C) are standardly taught as the dominant theme of Wuthering Heights. The case for love is that the Heathcliff and Catherine passion is the novel's core and the source of everything that follows; the case for revenge is that Heathcliff's revenge on Hindley, Edgar and the second generation drives most of the plot after his return. Nigerian study guides commonly list both, often together as 'love and revenge', and nothing in the stem favours one. A well-prepared student could not tell which the setter wanted, so the question should not carry a single key.

36.reason: Both nostalgic (A) and critical (D) are directly supported by the extract. The first four lines look back wistfully at the tree that 'once stood', shedding incense and lit by 'the last fires of a tribe', which is plainly nostalgic. The closing lines condemn the surveyors and builders and their 'huge, senseless cathedral of doom', which is plainly critical. Neither reading is strained, and study notes on this poem describe its tone both ways, so a well-prepared student could not tell which the setter intended.
